paragraphs.text: The plural in German sits on the noun itself, not on a word in front of it, and it is allowed to reach into the word and change its vowels. That is the whole reason a noun is worth carrying as a pair rather than as a single form.
der Arzt → die Ärzte · das Buch → die Bücher · die Stunde → die Stunden · der Kilometer → die Kilometer

Five endings cover almost everything you will meet at this level: nothing at all ({{de:der Kilometer → die Kilometer}}), {{de:-(e)n}}, {{de:-e}} with a vowel change ({{de:Arzt → Ärzte}}), {{de:-er}} with a change ({{de:Buch → Bücher}}) and {{de:-s}} for words borrowed from other languages ({{de:das Auto → die Autos}}).

The article tells you as much as the ending does, and it hands you the simplest rule on the page. Whatever a noun was in the singular, the plural stands in front of exactly one article — {{de:die}} — never {{de:der}} and never {{de:das}}.
der Tag → die Tage · das Restaurant → die Restaurants · die Ärztin → die Ärztinnen

Most job names in German come in two forms, and the second form does more than swap a word — it changes the article with it. The man is {{de:der Informatiker}}; add the ending that marks a woman and you get {{de:die Informatikerin}}.

You have already met this pair working: {{de:der Arzt}} beside {{de:die Ärztin}}, {{de:der Taxifahrer}} beside a driver who would be {{de:die Taxifahrerin}}. Notice that the plural then stacks on top — {{de:die Ärztinnen}} — so the woman's form carries two marks instead of one.
When you write a job on a form or say what you do, pick the pair deliberately. The noun tells your listener not only what the person does, but who the person is.

Two verbs appear in almost every sentence you have read so far, and both of them refuse to follow the -e, -st, -t pattern. They swap their stems instead, which means the forms have to be taken as whole blocks rather than assembled.
ich bin · du bist · er/sie/es ist · wir sind · ihr seid · sie/Sie sind
ich habe · du hast · er/sie/es hat · wir haben · ihr habt · sie/Sie haben
You need them for exactly the two questions this page practises: what somebody does for a living is asked with {{de:sein}}, and free time is asked with {{de:haben}}.
Was sind Sie von Beruf? — Wann haben Sie frei?
Learn the four singular forms first and the plural rows come free, because {{de:wir}}, {{de:sie}} and {{de:Sie}} share one form in each verb. Only {{de:ihr}} stands apart.

blocks.englishBridge: English says I am, you are, he is — one word in three clothes — while German changes the word itself: bin, bist, ist.

concept.title: Nomen: Singular und Plural
concept.rule: A plural noun always takes die, and the ending lands on the noun itself: -n, -e, -er, -s or nothing at all, sometimes with a vowel change inside the word.
concept.exampleGerman: der Arzt → die Ärzte · das Auto → die Autos
concept.exampleEnglish: the doctor → the doctors · the car → the cars
